summary: Defines a certificate profile for Qualified Certificates, based on RFC 2459, used for identifying a person, with a general syntax that does not depend on local legal rules. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 3739.

eli5.summary: This is a standard format for a digital ID card that can be used in legal-style signatures. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: how are qualified certificates used for legal signatures
what extensions do qualified certificates require
subtitle: Standard digital ID certificates for legally-significant signatures and identification.

tldr.problem: Different countries and legal systems needed a common way to define digital certificates intended for legal signatures and high-assurance identification, with uniform syntax that works across jurisdictions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3039 profiles the X.509 certificate format to require certain fields (issuer and subject names) and five specific extensions (biometric data, qualified certificate statements, key usage, and others) suitable for legal use.
tldr.outcome: This provided a standard format for legally-binding digital IDs, though the specification was updated by RFC 3739 to better align with evolving legal and technical requirements.

facts.label: Number of required extensions
facts.value: 5 (policies, key usage, subject directory attributes, biometric info, QC statements)

facts.label: Name attributes minimum
facts.value: At least one of: commonName, givenName, or pseudonym

today: RFC 3039 was obsoleted by RFC 3739, which provides updated requirements and mechanisms for Qualified Certificates that better reflect evolving legal and technical standards.

sections.title: Introduction to Qualified Certificates
sections.content:
A Qualified Certificate is a digital certificate issued to a person (not an organization) that serves a legal purpose for digital signatures and identification with high assurance. This specification builds on the Internet X.509 PKI standard defined in RFC 2459.

Unlike general-purpose certificates, Qualified Certificates are specifically designed to meet legal and regulatory requirements across different jurisdictions. They are issued only to natural persons (living humans) and carry explicit statements about their qualified status, making them suitable for signatures that have legal force.
sections.eli5: A Qualified Certificate is like an official digital ID card for a person that can be used to sign important documents legally. It works the same way in different countries.

sections.title: Requirements and Design Principles
sections.content:
RFC 3039 defines key properties that Qualified Certificates must have: they are issued only to natural persons, by a CA that publicly states it issues Qualified Certificates, with a certificate policy that reflects the CA's practices and liabilities. The certificate must contain an identity based on either a person's real name, a pseudonym, or a common name.

The specification is intentionally general, with syntax that does not depend on local laws, but designed to allow further refinement for specific legal systems. Each relying party (someone verifying the certificate) may need to consult the CA's certificate policy or certification practice statement to understand the full legal implications.

Distinguished names (the formal identifiers) must be unique within each CA's domain for the entire lifetime of the CA, ensuring no two people get identical identities from the same issuer.
sections.eli5: These certificates are only for real people, not companies. Each CA promises it checked carefully. The format is the same everywhere, but each country can add its own rules on top.

sections.title: Certificate Fields and Identity Information
sections.content:
The RFC profiles two main certificate fields. The issuer field identifies the organization issuing the certificate using attributes like country, organization, locality, and serial number.

The subject field contains the identity of the person being certified. It MUST include at least one of: a commonName, a givenName, or a pseudonym. Additional attributes like surname, organizationName, postal address, and state can provide context. Each implementation must be able to interpret these attributes correctly.

Other attributes may be present but must not be necessary to distinguish one subject from another within the issuer's domain. This ensures uniqueness while allowing flexibility in how identities are represented.
sections.eli5: The certificate says who issued it (like a company name) and who owns it (like a person's name or nickname). Different formats work as long as each person gets a unique ID from the same issuer.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions for Legal Use
sections.content:
Qualified Certificates require five key extensions beyond the basic X.509 format:

Subject Directory Attributes store additional person information like date of birth, place of birth, gender, country of citizenship and residence, and job title. These complement the subject name and support authorization decisions.

Certificate Policies extensions indicate the policy or policies under which the certificate was issued, reflecting the CA's practices and procedures. This MUST be present.

Key Usage extension MUST be present and specifies what the key can be used for. For non-repudiation (proving the holder signed something), this bit typically appears alone.

Biometric Information extension stores a hash of a biometric template (such as a photograph or handwritten signature) to authenticate the identity of the subject. The actual biometric data is not stored in the certificate itself.

Qualified Certificate Statements extension contains declarations by the issuer that the certificate is indeed a Qualified Certificate under the specified legal system or jurisdiction. This can include maximum reliance limits on the CA's liability.
sections.eli5: The certificate includes extra spaces for personal data like birth date, a statement that it is a Qualified Certificate, and a check (hash) of a photo or signature to verify it is the right person.

sections.title: Security and Legal Context
sections.content:
The security of a Qualified Certificate depends heavily on how the private key is protected. CAs should not issue Qualified Certificates unless the private key is under the sole control of the subject and protected against misuse. The CA must verify that the public key legitimately represents the subject.

The nonRepudiation key usage bit should not be combined with other key usage bits, as mixing these has security implications.

Comparing two Qualified Certificates to determine if they represent the same person is complex and depends on understanding the semantics of the names used. Different CAs may interpret the same attributes differently, so direct comparison without understanding these semantics can be misleading.

RFC 3039 is a profile of RFC 2459, and all the security considerations from that document apply here as well.
sections.eli5: The private key must be kept safe and only by the real person. To check if two certificates are for the same person, you need to understand what each CA means by the names they use.
